Abstract.

Denote by 𝒫log\mathcal{P}_{\log} the set of all non-constant Pick functions ff whose logarithmic derivatives f′/ff^{\,\prime}/f also belong to the Pick class. Let 𝒰⁡(Λ)\mathcal{U}(\Lambda) be the family of functions z⋅f⁡(z)z\cdot f(z), where f∈𝒫logf\in\mathcal{P}_{\log} and ff is holomorphic on Λ:=ℂ∖[1,+∞)\Lambda:={\mathbb{C}}\setminus[1,+\infty). Important examples of functions in 𝒰⁡(Λ)\mathcal{U}(\Lambda) are the classical polylogarithms L​iα​(z)Li_{\alpha}(z) :⁣=:= ∑k=1∞zk/kα\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}z^{k}/k^{\alpha} for α≥0\alpha\geq 0, see [6](2015).

In this note we prove that every φ∈𝒰⁡(Λ)\varphi\in\mathcal{U}(\Lambda) is universally starlike, i.e., φ\varphi maps every circular domain in Λ\Lambda containing the origin one-to-one onto a starlike domain. Furthermore, we show that every non-constant function f∈𝒫logf\in\mathcal{P}_{\log} belongs to the Hardy space HpH_{p} on the upper half-plane for some constant p=p⁡(f)>1p=p(f)>1, unless ff is proportional to some function (a−z)−θ(a-z)^{-\theta} with a∈ℝa\in{\mathbb{R}} and 0<θ≤10<\theta\leq 1. Finally we derive a necessary and sufficient condition on a real-valued function vv for which there exists f∈𝒫logf\in\mathcal{P}_{\log} such that v⁡(x)=limε↓0Im​f​(x+i​ε)v(x)=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow 0}{\rm{Im}}f(x+i\varepsilon) for almost all x∈ℝx\in{\mathbb{R}}.

Key words and phrases: 
Starlike, Pick and Harmonic functions; HpH_{p}-spaces; Boundary behavior

1. Introduction

1.1. Universally starlike functions

 

Universally starlike functions have been introduced in [37], [36] as analytic functions in the slit domain Λ:=ℂ∖[1,∞)\Lambda:={\mathbb{C}}\setminus[1,\infty) satisfying the following conditions: (i) f⁡(0)=f′​(0)−1=0f(0)=f^{\prime}(0)-1=0, (ii) ff is univalent in Λ\Lambda and maps any circular domain ℂ⊂Λ{\mathbb{C}}\subset\Lambda containing the origin onto a domain starlike with respect to the origin. In some subsequent papers this notion has been extended to other domains and classes of so-called (universally) prestarlike functions in Λ\Lambda of order α<1\alpha<1 have been introduced. The universally starlike functions correspond to the case α=1/2\alpha=1/2 and some interesting general properties and representations of those functions have been discovered. In particular, it turns out that these functions are necessarily Pick functions (in Λ\Lambda), and can be represented in terms of specific probability measures on the interval [0,1][0,1] (see below).

The main goal of this paper is to provide a complete characterization of the universally starlike functions, relying on the theory of Pick functions. The paper also contains many other results, which are interesting by themselves, regarding the Hardy classes HpH_{p} of the upper half-plane.

In 2009 St. Ruscheweyh, L. Salinas and T. Sugawa [37, Cor.1, p.289] proved that Ψ\Psi is universally starlike if and only if there exists μ∈ℳ+​(ℝ)\mu\in\mathcal{M}^{+}({\mathbb{R}}) such that μ⁡(ℝ)=1\mu({\mathbb{R}})=1, supp⁡μ⊆[0,1]\supp\mu\subseteq[0,1] and

Ψ⁡(z)z=exp(∫[0,1]log11−t​zdμ(t)),z∈ℂ∖[1,+∞),\frac{\Psi(z)}{z}=\exp\left(\int_{[0,1]}\log\frac{1}{1-tz}\,d\mu(t)\right)\,,\quad z\in{\mathbb{C}}\setminus[1,+\infty)\,, (1.1)

where the principal branch of the logarithm is taken, ℳ+​(ℝ)\mathcal{M}^{+}({\mathbb{R}}) denotes the cone of all non-negative Borel measures on ℝ{\mathbb{R}} which are finite on compact sets, and

supp⁡μ:={x∈ℝ∣μ⁡((,,,))>0​∀ε>0}.\supp\mu:=\left\{x\in{\mathbb{R}}\mid\mu\big((x-\varepsilon,\,x+\varepsilon)\big)>0\ \forall\varepsilon>0\right\}\,.

Let 𝒰⁡(Λ)\mathcal{U}(\Lambda) be the family of all functions z⋅f⁡(z)z\cdot f(z), where ff is holomorphic on Λ:=ℂ∖[1,+∞)\Lambda:={\mathbb{C}}\setminus[1,+\infty) and ff is a non-constant Pick function whose logarithmic derivative f′/ff^{\,\prime}/f also belong to the Pick class.

One of the main results of the present paper is that every function φ∈𝒰⁡(Λ)\varphi\in\mathcal{U}(\Lambda) is universally starlike, i.e., φ\varphi maps every circular domain in Λ\Lambda containing the origin one-to-one onto a starlike domain.

Let Hol⁡(D)\hol(D) denote the set of all holomorphic functions in D⊂ℂD\subset{\mathbb{C}}, C⁡(ℝ)C({\mathbb{R}}) the set of all functions continuous on ℝ{\mathbb{R}}, ℬ⁡(ℝ){\mathcal{B}}({\mathbb{R}}) the family of all Borel subsets of ℝ{\mathbb{R}}, ℍ:={z∈ℂ∣Im⁡z>0}{\mathbb{H}}:=\left\{z\in{\mathbb{C}}\mid\IM z>0\right\} and 𝔻:={z∈ℂ∣|z|<1}{\mathbb{D}}:=\left\{z\in{\mathbb{C}}\mid|z|<1\right\}.

For any 0<p<+∞0<p<+\infty we consider the Hardy spaces on the unit disk [24, p.68] and on the upper half plane [11, p. 168], [24, p. 112] as well

Hp​(𝔻)\displaystyle H_{p}({\mathbb{D}}) :={f∈Hol⁡(𝔻)∣‖f‖Hp​(𝔻)max⁡{1,p}:=sup0≤r<1∫−ππ|f⁡(rei​θ)|p​𝑑θ<+∞},\displaystyle:=\left\{f\in\hol({\mathbb{D}})\mid\|f\|_{H_{p}({\mathbb{D}})}^{\max\{1,p\}}:=\sup\limits_{0\leq r<1}\int_{-\pi}^{\,\pi}\left|f(re^{i\theta})\right|^{p}\,d\theta<+\infty\right\}\,,
Hp​(ℍ)\displaystyle H_{p}({\mathbb{H}}) :={f∈Hol⁡(ℍ)∣f𝔻​(w):=f⁡(i⁡(1−w)1+w)∈Hp​(𝔻)},\displaystyle:=\left\{f\in\hol({\mathbb{H}})\mid f_{{\mathbb{D}}}(w):=f\left(\frac{i(1-w)}{1+w}\right)\in H_{p}({\mathbb{D}})\right\}\,,
ℋp​(ℍ)\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{p}({\mathbb{H}}) :={f∈Hol⁡(ℍ)∣supy>0∫ℝ|f⁡(x+iy)|p​dx<+∞}⊂Hp​(ℍ).\displaystyle:=\left\{f\in\hol({\mathbb{H}})\mid\sup\limits_{y>0}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}}|f(x+iy)|^{p}\,dx<+\infty\right\}\subset H_{p}({\mathbb{H}})\,.

We also deal with the real space L∞​(ℝ)L_{\infty}({\mathbb{R}}) consisting of all Borel measurable real-valued functions ff defined on ℝ{\mathbb{R}} such that ‖f‖L∞​(ℝ):=inf{a>0∣m⁡({x∈ℝ∣|f⁡(x)|>a})=0}<+∞\|f\|_{L_{\infty}({\mathbb{R}})}:=\inf\left\{a>0\mid m\big(\{x\in{\mathbb{R}}\mid|f(x)|>a\}\big)=0\right\}<+\infty, where it is assumed that inf∅:=+∞\inf\emptyset:=+\infty and mm denotes the Lebesgue measure on the real line. Recall that two functions in L∞​(ℝ)L_{\infty}({\mathbb{R}}) are identified whenever they are equal almost everywhere with respect to the Lebesgue measure mm (in short: mm-a.e. or just ’almost everywhere’).

Let Ω⊂ℂ\Omega\subset{\mathbb{C}} be a domain containing the origin, Hol1⁡(Ω)\hol_{1}(\Omega) denote the class of functions in Hol⁡(Ω)\hol(\Omega) normalized by f⁡(0)=f′​(0)−1=0f(0)=f^{\prime}(0)-1=0 and Hol0⁡(Ω)\hol_{0}(\Omega) be the set of functions f∈Hol⁡(Ω)f\in\hol(\Omega) with f⁡(0)=1f(0)=1. A domain is referred to as circular when it is a disk or a half plane. A domain Ω\Omega is called a starlike with respect to the origin if a straight line segment connecting an arbitrary point in it with the origin is contained in Ω\Omega. A function Ψ\Psi is called universally starlike (with respect to the origin) if Ψ∈Hol1(ℂ∖[1,+∞))\Psi\in\hol_{1}({\mathbb{C}}\setminus[1,+\infty)) and every circular domain in ℂ∖[1,+∞){\mathbb{C}}\setminus[1,+\infty) containing the origin is mapped by Ψ\Psi one-to-one onto a starlike domain.

1.2. Pick functions

 

Let 𝒫{\mathcal{P}} denote the set of Pick functions, i.e. the set of holomorphic functions Φ\Phi on ℍ{\mathbb{H}} with non-negative imaginary part, extended to −ℍ-{\mathbb{H}} by means of Φ⁡(z)=Φ⁡(z¯)¯\Phi(z)=\overline{\Phi(\overline{z})} for z∈−ℍz\in-{\mathbb{H}}. Thus,

𝒫:={Φ∈Hol(ℂ∖ℝ)|Im⁡Φ⁡(z)Im⁡z≥0,z∈ℂ∖ℝ;Φ(z)=Φ⁡(z¯)¯,z∈−ℍ}.\mathcal{P}:=\left\{\Phi\in\hol({\mathbb{C}}\setminus{\mathbb{R}})\ \left|\quad\frac{\IM\Phi(z)}{\IM z}\geq 0\,,\ z\in{\mathbb{C}}\setminus{\mathbb{R}}\,;\ \Phi(z)=\overline{\Phi(\overline{z})}\,,\ z\in-{\mathbb{H}}\ \right.\right\}\,. (1.2)

It is known (see [8, p.31]) that every Φ∈𝒫\Phi\in\mathcal{P} is either a real constant or Im⁡Φ⁡(z)>0\IM\Phi(z)>0 for all z∈ℍz\in{\mathbb{H}}. Each function in the class 𝒫\mathcal{P} has a unique canonical representation of the form (see [10, Th.1, p.20], [39, Lem.2.1, p.23])

Φ⁡(z)=α​z+β+∫−∞+∞(1t−z−t1+t2)​𝑑σ​(t),z∈ℂ∖ℝ,\Phi(z)=\alpha z+\beta+\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\left(\frac{1}{t-z}-\frac{t}{1+t^{2}}\right)\,d\sigma(t)\,,\quad z\in{\mathbb{C}}\setminus{\mathbb{R}}\,, (1.3)

where α≥0\alpha\geq 0, β∈ℝ\beta\in{\mathbb{R}} and σ∈ℳ+​(ℝ)\sigma\in\mathcal{M}^{+}({\mathbb{R}}) for which ∫ℝ(1+t2)−1​𝑑σ​(t)\int_{{\mathbb{R}}}(1+t^{2})^{-1}\,d\sigma(t) is finite. Conversely, any function of the form (1.3) is in 𝒫\mathcal{P}. It has been proved in [10, Lem.2, p.26] that

Φ∈𝒫∩Hol((a,b))⇔suppσ⊂ℝ∖(a,b),\Phi\in\mathcal{P}\cap\hol\big(\,(a,b)\,\big)\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad\supp\sigma\subset{\mathbb{R}}\setminus(a,b)\,, (1.4)

where a,b∈ℝa,b\in{\mathbb{R}}, a<ba<b and σ\sigma is a measure corresponding to Φ\Phi by (1.3).

For arbitrary Φ∈𝒫∖{0}\Phi\in\mathcal{P}\setminus\{0\} we have log⁡Φ∈𝒫\log\Phi\in\mathcal{P} and any function

f∈log⁡𝒫:={log⁡Φ∣Φ∈𝒫∖{0}}⊂𝒫f\in\log\mathcal{P}:=\big\{\log\Phi\mid\Phi\in\mathcal{P}\setminus\{0\}\big\}\subset\mathcal{P}

can be uniquely represented in the form (see [10, p.27])

f⁡(z)=β+∫−∞+∞(1t−z−t1+t2)​ρ​(t)​𝑑t,z∈ℂ∖ℝ,f(z)=\beta+\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\left(\frac{1}{t-z}-\frac{t}{1+t^{2}}\right)\,\rho(t)\,dt\,,\quad z\in{\mathbb{C}}\setminus{\mathbb{R}}\,, (1.5)

where β∈ℝ\beta\in{\mathbb{R}} and ρ∈L∞​(ℝ)\rho\in L_{\infty}({\mathbb{R}}) satisfies 0≤ρ⁡(x)≤10\leq\rho(x)\leq 1 for almost all x∈ℝx\in{\mathbb{R}} with respect to the Lebesgue measure (in short: for almost all). Conversely, any function of the form (1.5) is in log⁡𝒫\log\mathcal{P}.

1.3. Boundary values of Pick functions

 

For arbitrary Φ∈𝒫∖{0}\Phi\in\mathcal{P}\setminus\{0\} we denote f:=log⁡Φ∈log⁡𝒫f:=\log\Phi\in\log\mathcal{P} and replace the upper half plane by the unit disk with the help of the change of variables

Φ𝔻​(w):=Φ⁡(i⁡(1−w)1+w),f𝔻​(w)=log⁡Φ𝔻​(w),w∈𝔻.\Phi_{{\mathbb{D}}}(w):=\Phi\left(\frac{i(1-w)}{1+w}\right)\,,\quad f_{{\mathbb{D}}}(w)=\log\Phi_{{\mathbb{D}}}(w)\,,\quad w\in{\mathbb{D}}\,.

Then the formula (1.5) can be rewritten as follows (cp.[24, p.76])

f𝔻​(w)=β+i2​∫−ππei​θ+wei​θ−w​ρ​(tan⁡θ2)​𝑑θ.f_{{\mathbb{D}}}(w)=\beta+\frac{i}{2}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{\,e^{i\theta}+w\,}{e^{i\theta}-w}\ \rho\left(\tan\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\;d\theta\,. (1.6)

In view of A.E. Plessner’s theorem [30, p.17] (see [42, Ex.24, p.245], [24, p.58]), f𝔻∈Hol⁡(𝔻)f_{{\mathbb{D}}}\in\hol({\mathbb{D}}) and Im⁡f𝔻≥0\IM f_{{\mathbb{D}}}\geq 0 in 𝔻{\mathbb{D}} imply that for almost all θ∈[−π,π]\theta\in[-\pi,\pi] there exists a finite limit f𝔻​(ei​θ)f_{{\mathbb{D}}}(e^{i\theta}) of f𝔻​(w)f_{{\mathbb{D}}}(w) as w∈𝔻w\in{\mathbb{D}} tends to ei​θe^{i\theta} non-tangentially (in short: w​⟶∠​ei​θw\overset{\angle}{\longrightarrow}e^{i\theta}) [24, p.11, 15]. Thus, for almost all x∈ℝx\in{\mathbb{R}} there exists the (non-tangential) finite boundary value f⁡(x+i​0):=limℍ∋z​→∠​xf⁡(z)f(x+i0):=\lim\limits_{{{\mathbb{H}}}\ni z\overset{\angle}{\rightarrow}x}f(z) and since f⁡(tan⁡θ2+i​ 0)=f𝔻​(ei​θ)f(\tan\frac{\theta}{2}+i\,0)=f_{{\mathbb{D}}}(e^{i\theta}), θ∈(−π,π)\theta\in(-\pi,\pi), in view of Fatou’s [24, p.11] and Titchmarsh’s [24, p.20] theorems we have

f⁡(tan⁡θ2+i​ 0)=i​π​ρ​(tan⁡θ2)+β+lim0<ε→0∫επρ⁡(tan⁡(θ+t)2)−ρ⁡(tan⁡(θ−t)2)2​tan⁡t2​𝑑tf\left(\tan{{\mbox{\large{$\frac{\theta}{\vphantom{A^{A^{a}}}2}$}}}}+i\,0\right)=i\pi\rho\left(\tan{{\mbox{\large{$\frac{\theta}{\vphantom{A^{A^{a}}}2}$}}}}\right)+\beta+\lim_{0<\varepsilon\to 0}\int_{\varepsilon}^{\pi}\frac{\rho\left(\tan{{\mbox{\large{$\frac{(\theta+t)}{\vphantom{A^{A^{a}}}2}$}}}}\right)-\rho\left(\tan{{\mbox{\large{$\frac{(\theta-t)}{\vphantom{A^{A^{a}}}2}$}}}}\right)}{2\tan{{\mbox{\large{$\frac{t}{\vphantom{A^{A^{a}}}2}$}}}}}\;dt (1.7)

for almost all θ∈(−π,π)\theta\in(-\pi,\pi). For the corresponding x∈ℝx\in{\mathbb{R}} the limit

Φ⁡(x+i​0):=limℍ∋z​→∠​xΦ⁡(z)=limℍ∋z​→∠​xef⁡(z)=ef⁡(x+i​0)\Phi(x+i0):=\lim_{{{\mathbb{H}}}\ni z\overset{\angle}{\rightarrow}x}\Phi(z)=\lim_{{\mathbb{H}}\ni z\overset{\angle}{\rightarrow}x}e^{f(z)}=e^{f(x+i0)}

exists and is finite. Moreover, as straightforward consequences of well-known results in the theory of HpH_{p}-spaces, it is established in subsection 3.1 below that (cp. [15, Lem. 6.2, p. 255])

∫ℝ|Φ⁡(x+i​0)|±δ1+x2​𝑑x<+∞,\displaystyle\int\nolimits_{{\mathbb{R}}}\frac{|\Phi(x+i0)|^{{{\mbox{\footnotesize{$\pm\delta$}}}}}}{1+x^{2}}\,dx<+\infty\,, δ∈(0,1),\displaystyle\quad\delta\in(0,1)\,, Φ∈𝒫∖{0},\displaystyle\quad\Phi\in\mathcal{P}\setminus\{0\}\,, (1.8)
∫ℝ|f⁡(x+i​0)|p+eδ​|f⁡(x+i​0)|1+x2​𝑑x<+∞,\displaystyle\int\nolimits_{{\mathbb{R}}}\frac{|f(x+i0)|^{{{\mbox{\footnotesize{$p$}}}}}+e^{\,{{\mbox{\footnotesize{$\delta|f(x+i0)|$}}}}}}{1+x^{2}}\;dx<+\infty\,, δ∈(0,1),\displaystyle\quad\delta\in(0,1)\,, p>0,f∈log⁡𝒫,\displaystyle\quad p>0\,,\quad f\in\log{\mathcal{P}}\,, (1.9)
𝒫⊂Hδ​(ℍ),log⁡𝒫⊂Hp​(ℍ),\displaystyle\mathcal{P}\subset H_{\delta}({\mathbb{H}})\,,\quad\log{\mathcal{P}}\subset H_{p}({\mathbb{H}})\,, δ∈(0,1),\displaystyle\quad\delta\in(0,1)\,, p>0.\displaystyle\quad p>0\,. (1.10)

It should be noted that inequality (1.9) cannot be improved to cover the case δ=1\delta=1 because Φ⁡(z)=z∈𝒫∖{0}\Phi(z)=z\in\mathcal{P}\setminus\{0\} and f⁡(z)=log⁡z∈log⁡𝒫f(z)=\log z\in\log{\mathcal{P}}.

Every Φ∈𝒫∖{0}\Phi\in\mathcal{P}\setminus\{0\} is an outer function for the class Hδ​(ℍ)H_{\delta}({\mathbb{H}}) for arbitrary δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) (see [11, Th.11.6, p.193]), as it follows from (1.8), (1.10) and the Schwarz integral formula [31, p.206] applied to the function log⁡Φ∈H1​(ℍ)\log\Phi\in H_{1}({\mathbb{H}}), which by [11, Th.3.1, p.34] can be represented as the Poisson integral

log⁡Φ⁡(x+i​y)=1π​∫ℝy​log⁡Φ​(t+i​0)(x−t)2+y2​𝑑t,x+i​y∈ℍ,Φ∈𝒫∖{0},\log\Phi(x+iy)=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}}\frac{\;y\,\log\Phi(t+i0)\;}{(x-t)^{2}+y^{2}}\;dt\,,\quad x+iy\in{\mathbb{H}}\,,\quad\Phi\in\mathcal{P}\setminus\{0\}\,,

of its boundary values log⁡Φ⁡(x+i​0)\log\Phi(x+i0). Thus, in addition to the exponential representation Φ=ef\Phi=e^{f} with f=log⁡Φf=\log\Phi given by (1.5) with π​ρ​(t)=arg⁡Φ⁡(t+i​0)\pi\rho(t)=\arg\Phi(t+i0), any Φ∈𝒫∖{0}\Phi\in\mathcal{P}\setminus\{0\} has also another one, namely

Φ⁡(z)=exp⁡(1π​i​∫−∞+∞(1t−z−t1+t2)​log⁡|Φ⁡(t+i​0)|​𝑑t+i​arg⁡Φ⁡(i)),z∈ℍ,Φ∈𝒫∖{0}.\Phi(z)=\exp\left({{\mbox{\large{$\frac{1}{\vphantom{A^{A^{a}}}\pi i}$}}}}\int\limits_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\left({{\mbox{\large{$\frac{1}{\vphantom{A^{A^{a}}}t-z}$}}}}-{{\mbox{\large{$\frac{t}{\vphantom{A^{A^{a}}}1+t^{2}}$}}}}\right)\,\log|\Phi(t+i0)|\;dt+i\arg\Phi(i)\right)\,,\quad z\in{\mathbb{H}}\,,\quad\Phi\in\mathcal{P}\setminus\{0\}\,.

It is well-known (see [24, p.100], [14, Cor.2.6, p.114]) that if g∈C⁡(ℝ)g\in C({\mathbb{R}}) is periodic with period 2​π2\pi, then

∫−ππep⋅|g~​(θ)|​𝑑θ<+∞for all​p>0,\int_{-\pi}^{\,\pi}e^{\ {{\mbox{\footnotesize{$p\cdot|\widetilde{g}(\theta)|$}}}}}\;d\theta<+\infty\quad\text{for all}\ p>0\,, (1.11)

where (cp. [24, p.89])

g~​(θ):=lim0<ε→01π​∫επg⁡(θ+t)−g⁡(θ−t)2​tan⁡t2​𝑑t.\widetilde{g}(\theta):=\lim\limits_{0<\varepsilon\to 0}\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{\varepsilon}^{\pi}\frac{g(\theta+t)-g(\theta-t)}{2\tan{{\mbox{\large{$\frac{t}{\vphantom{A^{A^{a}}}2}$}}}}}\;dt\,. (1.12)

Therefore, (1.6) and (1.7) yield (compare with (1.9))

∫ℝeq⋅|f⁡(x+i​0)|1+x2​𝑑x<+∞,q>0,\int_{{\mathbb{R}}}\frac{e^{\ {{\mbox{\footnotesize{$q\cdot|f(x+i0)|$}}}}}}{1+x^{2}}\;dx<+\infty\,,\quad q>0\,, (1.13)

provided that f∈log⁡𝒫f\in\log\mathcal{P} and the function ρ\rho corresponding to ff in (1.5) satisfies ρ⁡(tan⁡x2)∈C⁡(ℝ)\rho(\tan{{\mbox{\large{$\frac{x}{\vphantom{A^{A^{a}}}2}$}}}})\in C({\mathbb{R}}).

It is easily verified (see 3.2) that the power of exponent in the righthand side of (1.1) can be converted to the following expression

Denote the set of all primitives of the functions in 𝒫\mathcal{P} as follows

2. Main Results

In order to formulate the main theorems it is first necessary to introduce some notations for the Lebesgue-Stieltjes measures and integrals.

2.1. Notation for measures and non-decreasing functions on the real line

 

Denote by M↑​(E)M^{\uparrow}(E) the family of all non-decreasing on E⊂ℝE\subset{\mathbb{R}} functions ϕ:E→ℝ\phi:E\to{\mathbb{R}}. Consider an arbitrary ϕ∈M↑​(ℝ)\phi\in M^{\uparrow}({\mathbb{R}}) and the Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure ωϕ∈ℳ+​(ℝ)\omega_{\phi}\in\mathcal{M}^{+}({\mathbb{R}}) induced by ϕ\phi\, [27, Def. 3.9, p.147]. It is worth reminding that at every x∈ℝx\in{\mathbb{R}} the left- and the right-hand side limits exist and both are finite:

−∞<ϕ⁡(x−0):=limt↑xϕ⁡(t)≤ϕ⁡(x)≤limt↓xϕ⁡(t)=:ϕ⁡(x+0)<+∞.-\infty<\phi(x-0):=\lim_{t\uparrow x}\phi(t)\leq\phi(x)\leq\lim_{t\downarrow x}\phi(t)=:\phi(x+0)<+\infty.

Moreover, the set of points of discontinuity of ϕ\phi,

Dϕ={x∈ℝ∣ϕ⁡(x−0)<ϕ⁡(x+0)},ϕ∈M↑​(ℝ),D_{\phi}=\big\{x\in{\mathbb{R}}\mid\phi(x-0)<\phi(x+0)\big\}\,,\quad\phi\in M^{\uparrow}({\mathbb{R}})\,, (2.1)

is at most countable [19, Th.8.19, p.111].

The mapping ℒ𝒮\mathcal{L_{S}} of M↑​(ℝ)M^{\uparrow}({\mathbb{R}}) onto ℳ+​(ℝ)\mathcal{M}^{+}({\mathbb{R}})\,, ϕ↦ωϕ\phi\mapsto\omega_{\phi} (cf. [13, Th.1.16, p.35]), determines a partition of M↑​(ℝ)M^{\uparrow}({\mathbb{R}}) into disjoint sets

{ℒ𝒮−1​(μ)∣μ∈ℳ+​(ℝ)}={Γϕ∣ϕ∈M↑​(ℝ)},\left\{\mathcal{L_{S}}^{-1}(\mu)\mid\mu\in\mathcal{M}^{+}({\mathbb{R}})\right\}=\left\{\Gamma_{\phi}\mid\phi\in M^{\uparrow}({\mathbb{R}})\right\}\,,

where

Γϕ={b+ψ∣b∈ℝ,ψ∈ℵϕ},\Gamma_{\phi}=\big\{b+\psi\mid b\in{\mathbb{R}}\,,\ \psi\in\aleph_{\phi}\big\}\,,

and

ℵϕ={ψ∈M↑(ℝ)∣ψ(x)∈[ϕ(x−0),ϕ(x+0)],x∈ℝ},ϕ∈M↑(ℝ),\aleph_{\phi}=\big\{\psi\in M^{\uparrow}({\mathbb{R}})\mid\psi(x)\in[\phi(x-0),\,\phi(x+0)]\,,\;x\in{\mathbb{R}}\big\}\,,\qquad\phi\in M^{\uparrow}({\mathbb{R}})\,, (2.2)

(see [27, Prop. 3.9(v), p.145], [20, p. 551]). We now assume that the closure of E⊆ℝE\subseteq{\mathbb{R}} in ℝ{\mathbb{R}} is equal to ℝ{\mathbb{R}} and f∈M↑​(ℝ)f\in M^{\uparrow}({\mathbb{R}}). Then it is easily verified that

from which we get

ℵϕ\displaystyle\aleph_{\phi} =\displaystyle= {ψ∈M↑​(ℝ)∣ψ=ϕ​m-a.e. on ℝ},\displaystyle\big\{\psi\in M^{\uparrow}({\mathbb{R}})\mid\psi=\phi\ \text{$m$-a.e. on ${\mathbb{R}}$}\;\big\}\,,\quad ϕ∈M↑​(ℝ),\displaystyle\phi\in M^{\uparrow}({\mathbb{R}})\,, (2.4)
Dψ\displaystyle D_{\psi} =\displaystyle= Dϕ,ψ⁡(−∞)=ϕ⁡(−∞),ψ∈ℵϕ,\displaystyle D_{\phi}\,,\quad\psi(-\infty)=\phi(-\infty)\,,\quad\psi\in\aleph_{\phi}\,,\quad ϕ∈M↑​(ℝ),\displaystyle\phi\in M^{\uparrow}({\mathbb{R}})\,, (2.5)

irrespective of whether ϕ⁡(−∞):=limt→−∞ϕ⁡(t)\phi(-\infty):=\lim_{\,t\to-\infty}\phi(t) is finite or equal to −∞-\infty. It follows from (2.2) that for each ϕ∈M↑​(ℝ)\phi\in M^{\uparrow}({\mathbb{R}}) the functions in the class ℵϕ\aleph_{\,\phi} are equal to each other everywhere except at most at countable many points in DϕD_{\phi} and (cf. [7, Ex.2, p.156]) ℵϕ\aleph_{\phi} contains a unique function ψ\psi satisfying

If [a,b]⊂ℝ[a,b]\subset{\mathbb{R}} is a bounded interval and gg is an absolutely continuous function on [a,b][a,b] then the formula of integration by parts (cf. [7, p.166], [9, Th.6.2.2, p.100], [27, Prop.4.9, p.202; Cor.4.3, p.214]) gives

∫[a,b]g⁡(x)​d​ωϕ​(x)=g⁡(b)​ϕ​(b+0)−g⁡(a)​ϕ​(a−0)−∫abϕ⁡(x)​g′​(x)​𝑑x.\int_{[a,b]}g(x)\,d\omega_{\phi}(x)=g(b)\,\phi(b+0)-g(a)\,\phi(a-0)-\int_{a}^{b}\phi(x)\,g^{\prime}(x)\,dx\,. (2.7)

When μ∈ℳ+​(ℝ)\mu\in\mathcal{M}^{+}({\mathbb{R}}) is given, we also denote by μ\mu any of those functions in ℒ𝒮−1​(μ)⊂M↑​(ℝ)\mathcal{L_{S}^{{\rm{-1}}}}(\mu)\subset M^{\uparrow}({\mathbb{R}}) which satisfy (2.6). But, if μ\mu is finite, we additionally assume that μ⁡(−∞)=0\mu(-\infty)=0, i.e.

2.2. The classes 𝒫∫∩𝒫{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}\cap\mathcal{P} and 𝒫∫∩log⁡𝒫{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}\cap\log{\mathcal{P}}

 

We recall that any harmonic function in ℍ{\mathbb{H}} is analytic in ℍ{\mathbb{H}} (see [18, Th.1.15, p.31]) and, in particular, all its partial derivatives of any order are continuous functions in ℍ{\mathbb{H}}. The following assertion is of independent interest.

Theorem 2.1.

Let V⁡(x,y)V(x,y) be a harmonic function in ℍ{{\mathbb{H}}} and

V⁡(x,y)≥0,Vx​(x,y)≥0,y>0,x∈ℝ.V(x,y)\geq 0\,,\quad V_{x}(x,y)\geq 0\,,\quad y>0\,,\quad x\in{\mathbb{R}}\,. (2.8)

Then the following statements hold:

1. There exist a finite constant α≥0\alpha\geq 0 and a non-negative non-decreasing function ν\nu on ℝ{\mathbb{R}} such that

∫1+∞ν⁡(t)t2​𝑑t<+∞,\int_{1}^{+\infty}\frac{\nu(t)}{t^{2}}\,dt<+\infty\,, (2.9)

and

V⁡(x,y)=α​y+∫−∞+∞yy2+(x−t)2​ν​(t)​𝑑t,y>0,x∈ℝ.V(x,y)=\alpha y+\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\frac{y}{y^{2}+(x-t)^{2}}\;\nu(t)\,dt\,,\quad y>0\,,\quad x\in{\mathbb{R}}\,. (2.10)

Conversely, any function of this form is harmonic in ℍ{{\mathbb{H}}} and satisfies conditions (2.8). The representation (2.10) is unique if we identify non-decreasing functions that are equal almost everywhere on ℝ{\mathbb{R}} (see (2.4), (2.2)).

2. Either Vx​(x,y)>0V_{x}(x,y)>0 or Vx​(x,y)≡0V_{x}(x,y)\equiv 0 for any y>0y>0, x∈ℝx\in{\mathbb{R}}, and the latter case holds if and only if the function ν\nu in (2.10) is a non-negative constant function ν⁡(x)≡a≥0\nu(x)\equiv a\geq 0, or, what is the same, V⁡(x,y)=α​y+a⋅πV(x,y)=\alpha y+a\cdot\pi, y>0y>0, x∈ℝx\in{\mathbb{R}}, with some α,a≥0\alpha,a\geq 0.

Since in all the statements below the subclasses of 𝒫∖{0}\mathcal{P}\setminus\{0\} are considered, we introduce the following general notations.

For arbitrary f∈𝒫∖{0}f\in{\mathcal{P}}\setminus\{0\} denote

Uf​(x,y):=Re⁡f⁡(x+iy),Vf​(x,y):=Im⁡f⁡(x+iy),x∈ℝ,y>0.U^{f}(x,y):=\RE f(x+iy)\,,\quad V^{f}(x,y):=\IM f(x+iy)\,,\quad x\in{\mathbb{R}}\,,\quad y>0\,.

m⁡(ℝ∖𝒟⁡(f))=m⁡(ℝ∖𝒟⁡(Uf))=m⁡(ℝ∖𝒟⁡(Vf))=0,𝒟⁡(f):=𝒟⁡(Uf)∩𝒟⁡(Vf),m\left({\mathbb{R}}\setminus\mathcal{D}(f)\right)=m\left({\mathbb{R}}\setminus\mathcal{D}(U^{f})\right)=m\left({\mathbb{R}}\setminus\mathcal{D}(V^{f})\right)=0\,,\quad\mathcal{D}(f):=\mathcal{D}(U^{f})\cap\mathcal{D}(V^{f})\,, (2.11)

Theorem 2.1 gives rise to a canonical representation of the functions in the class 𝒫∩𝒫∫\mathcal{P}\cap{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int} which, in turn, leads to explicit expressions for their boundary values.

Theorem 2.2.

Let 𝒫∫∩𝒫{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}\cap\mathcal{P} be defined as in (1.15).

1. A function Φ\Phi belongs to the class 𝒫∫∩𝒫{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}\cap\mathcal{P} if and only if there exist constants α≥0\alpha\geq 0, β∈ℝ\beta\in{\mathbb{R}} and a non-negative non-decreasing function ν\nu on ℝ{\mathbb{R}} satisfying

The limit of VΦ​(x,y)V^{\Phi}(x,y) as y→0y\to 0, y>0y>0 (in short: y↓0y\downarrow 0), exists and is finite for every x∈ℝx\in{\mathbb{R}} and

VΦ​(x,0+0):=limy↓0VΦ​(x,y)=π​ν​(x),V^{\Phi}(x,0+0):=\lim_{y\downarrow 0}V^{\Phi}(x,y)=\pi\nu(x)\ , (2.19)

provided that ν\nu satisfies (2.6). In addition, 𝒟⁡(VΦ)⊂ℝ∖Dν\mathcal{D}(V^{\Phi})\subset{\mathbb{R}}\setminus D_{\nu} (see (2.1), (2.11)).

Some important particular cases of functions from the class 𝒫∩𝒫∫\mathcal{P}\cap{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int} are considered in the following corollary.

Corollary 2.1.

The first derivative of any function Φ∈𝒫∩𝒫∫\Phi\in\mathcal{P}\cap{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int} with integral representation (2.14) can be expressed as:

Φ′​(z)=α+∫−∞+∞d​ν​(t)t−z,z∈ℍ.\Phi^{\,\prime}(z)=\alpha+\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\frac{d\nu(t)}{t-z}\,,\quad z\in{\mathbb{H}}\,. (2.20)

and the following assertions hold:

  • (i)

    If Φ\Phi is a constant function, then α=0\alpha=0, ν⁡(x)≡ν⁡(−∞)≥0\nu(x)\equiv\nu(-\infty)\geq 0 and thus,
    Φ⁡(z)≡β+i​π⋅ν⁡(−∞)\Phi(z)\equiv\beta+i\pi\cdot\nu(-\infty), Im⁡Φ⁡(z)≡π⋅ν⁡(−∞)≥0\IM\Phi(z)\equiv\pi\cdot\nu(-\infty)\geq 0, Φ′​(z)≡0\Phi^{\,\prime}(z)\equiv 0.

  • (ii)

    If ν\nu is a constant function, i.e. ν⁡(x)≡ν⁡(−∞)≥0\nu(x)\equiv\nu(-\infty)\geq 0, then Φ⁡(z)=α​z+β+i​π⋅ν⁡(−∞)\Phi(z)=\alpha z+\beta+i\pi\cdot\nu(-\infty) and Φ′​(z)≡α\Phi^{\,\prime}(z)\equiv\alpha, Im⁡Φ′​(z)≡0\IM\Phi^{\,\prime}(z)\equiv 0.

  • (iii)

    If Φ\Phi is not a linear function, then Im⁡Φ⁡(z)>0\IM\Phi(z)>0 and Im⁡Φ′​(z)>0\IM\Phi^{\,\prime}(z)>0 for each z∈ℍz\in{\mathbb{H}}.

It follows from [21, Th. 2, p.143] and (2.20) that:

∫1+∞Im⁡Φ′​(it)t​𝑑t<+∞for every Φ∈𝒫∩𝒫∫.\int_{1}^{+\infty}\frac{\IM\Phi^{\,\prime}(it)}{t}\,dt<+\infty\quad\text{for every $\Phi\in\mathcal{P}\cap{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}$}\,.

A direct application of Theorem 2.2, with the additional restriction that Φ∈log⁡𝒫⊂𝒫\Phi\in\log{\mathcal{P}}\subset\mathcal{P}, yields a canonical representation of all functions in 𝒫∫∩log⁡𝒫⊂𝒫∫∩𝒫{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}\cap\log\mathcal{P}\subset{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}\cap\mathcal{P}, with an explicit expressions for their boundary values.

Theorem 2.3.

Let 𝒫∫∩log⁡𝒫{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}\cap\log\mathcal{P} be defined as in (1.16). Every function ff in the class 𝒫∫∩log⁡𝒫{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}\cap\log\mathcal{P} admits a canonical representation of the form

f⁡(z)=β+∫−∞+∞(1t−z−t1+t2)​ν​(t)​𝑑t,z∈ℂ∖ℝ,f(z)=\beta+\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\left(\frac{1}{t-z}-\frac{t}{1+t^{2}}\right)\,\nu(t)\,dt\,,\quad z\in{\mathbb{C}}\setminus{\mathbb{R}}\,, (2.21)

or, what is the same,

f⁡(z)=β+i​π​ν​(−∞)+∫−∞+∞log⁡1+t2t−z​𝑑ν​(t),z∈ℍ,f(z)=\beta+i\pi\nu(-\infty)+\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\log\frac{\sqrt{1+t^{2}}}{t-z}\,d\nu(t)\,,\quad z\in{\mathbb{H}}\,, (2.22)

where the principal branch of the logarithm is taken, β∈ℝ\beta\in{\mathbb{R}} and ν\nu is a non-decreasing function on ℝ{\mathbb{R}} satisfying

0≤ν(x1)≤ν(x2)≤1,x1<x2,x1,x2∈ℝ.0\leq\nu(x_{1})\leq\nu(x_{2})\leq 1\,,\quad x_{1}<x_{2}\,,\quad x_{1},x_{2}\in{\mathbb{R}}\,. (2.23)

Conversely, any function of the form (2.21) or (2.22) with a non-decreasing function ν\nu on ℝ{\mathbb{R}} satisfying (2.23) belongs to 𝒫∫∩log⁡𝒫{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}\cap\log\mathcal{P}. The representations (2.21) and (2.22) are unique if we identify the non-decreasing functions that are equal almost everywhere on ℝ{\mathbb{R}} (see (2.2), (2.4), (2.5)).

For almost all x∈ℝx\in{\mathbb{R}} we have log⁡1+t2|t−x|∈L1​(ℝ,d​ν​(t))\log{{\mbox{\large{$\frac{\sqrt{1+t^{2}}}{\vphantom{A^{A^{a}}}|t-x|}$}}}}\in L_{1}({\mathbb{R}},d\nu(t)) and

Uf​(x)=β+∫−∞+∞log⁡1+t2|t−x|​𝑑ν​(t).U^{f}(x)=\beta+\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\log\frac{\sqrt{1+t^{2}}}{|t-x|}\,d\nu(t)\,. (2.24)

Whenever ν\nu satisfies (2.6), then

Vf​(x,0+0):=limy↓0Vf​(x,y)=π​ν​(x),for every x∈ℝ.V^{f}(x,0+0):=\lim_{y\downarrow 0}V^{f}(x,y)=\pi\nu(x)\,,\quad\text{for every $x\in{\mathbb{R}}$}\,. (2.25)

Furthermore, for f∈𝒫∫∩log⁡𝒫f\in{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}\cap\log\mathcal{P} the following holds:

  • (i)

    The function ff is identically constant if and only if ν\nu is a constant function.

  • (ii)

    If ff is a constant function, then f⁡(z)=β+i​π​θf(z)=\beta+i\pi\theta and ν⁡(x)≡θ\nu(x)\equiv\theta, where β∈ℝ\beta\in{\mathbb{R}} and θ∈[0,1]\theta\in[0,1].

  • (iii)

    If ff is a non-constant function, then Im⁡f⁡(z)>0\IM f(z)>0 and Im⁡f′​(z)>0\IM f^{\prime}(z)>0 for each z∈ℍz\in{\mathbb{H}}.

It obviously follows from (2.21) and (2.22) that for arbitrary f∈𝒫∫∩log⁡𝒫f\in{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}\cap\log\mathcal{P}, y>0y>0 and x∈ℝx\in{\mathbb{R}} the following equalities hold:

Uf​(x,y)\displaystyle U^{f}(x,y) =β+∫−∞+∞(t−xy2+(x−t)2−t1+t2)​ν​(t)​𝑑t\displaystyle=\beta+\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\left(\frac{t-x}{y^{2}+(x-t)^{2}}-\frac{t}{1+t^{2}}\right)\,\nu(t)\,dt
=β+∫−∞+∞log⁡1+t2y2+(t−x)2​𝑑ν​(t),\displaystyle=\beta+\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\log\sqrt{\frac{1+t^{2}}{y^{2}+(t-x)^{2}}}\,d\nu(t)\,,
Vf​(x,y)\displaystyle V^{f}(x,y) =∫−∞+∞yy2+(x−t)2​ν​(t)​𝑑t\displaystyle=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\frac{y}{y^{2}+(x-t)^{2}}\,\nu(t)\,dt
=π​ν​(−∞)+∫−∞+∞(π2−arctan⁡t−xy)​𝑑ν​(t).\displaystyle=\pi\nu(-\infty)+\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\arctan\frac{t-x}{y}\right)\,d\nu(t)\,.

The following fact follows easily from Theorem 2.3.

Corollary 2.2.

f∈𝒫∫∩log⁡𝒫∩Hol⁡((−∞,1))f\in{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}\cap\log\mathcal{P}\cap\hol((-\infty,1)) if and only if there exists some μ∈ℳ+​(ℝ)\mu\in\mathcal{M}^{+}({\mathbb{R}}) with supp⁡μ⊆[0,1]\supp\mu\subseteq[0,1] and μ⁡(ℝ)=1\mu({\mathbb{R}})=1, such that

f⁡(z)=∫[0,1]log⁡11−t​z​𝑑μ​(t),z∈ℍ.f(z)=\int_{[0,1]}\log\frac{1}{1-tz}\,d\mu(t)\,,\quad z\in{\mathbb{H}}\,. (2.26)

According to the definition (1.16) and Theorem 2.3 a non-constant function ff belongs to the class 𝒫∫∩log⁡𝒫{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}\cap\log\mathcal{P} if and only if for every x+i​y∈ℍx+iy\in{\mathbb{H}}, 0<Vf​(x,y)<π0<V^{f}(x,y)<\pi and Vxf​(x,y)>0V_{x}^{f}(x,y)>0. Thus, a non-constant function ff belongs to the class 𝒫∫∩log⁡𝒫{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}\cap\log\mathcal{P} if and only if any one (and therefore all) of the following conditions hold:

{(a)0<V⁡(x1,y)<V⁡(x2,y)<π,−∞<x1<x2<+∞,y>0,(b)U(x,y2)<U(x,y1), 0<V(x,y)<π,<y1<y2<+∞,y>0,x∈ℝ.\hskip-14.22636pt\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}(a)&0<V(x_{1},y)<V(x_{2},y)<\pi\,,&-\infty\!<\!x_{1}\!<\!x_{2}\!<\!+\infty\,,&y\!>\!0\,,\\[8.5359pt] (b)&U(x,y_{2})<U(x,y_{1})\,,\ 0<V(x,y)<\pi\,,&0\!<\!y_{1}\!<\!y_{2}\!<\!+\infty\,,&y\!>\!0\,,\ x\!\in\!{\mathbb{R}}\,.\end{array}\right.\hskip-4.26773pt (2.27)

Indeed, the inequalities in the left-hand side of (2.27), (a) and (b), follow obviously from the inequalities Vxf​(x,y)>0V_{x}^{f}(x,y)>0 and Uyf​(x,y)<0U_{y}^{f}(x,y)<0, respectively. Conversely, (2.27), (a) and (b), imply that the harmonic functions Vxf​(x,y)V_{x}^{f}(x,y) and −Uyf​(x,y)-U_{y}^{f}(x,y) are non-constant and non-negative, which means that they are strictly positive in ℍ{\mathbb{H}} in view of the mean value property of harmonic functions [18, (1.5.4), p.34].

An exceptional position in the class 𝒫∫∩log⁡𝒫{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}\cap\log\mathcal{P} is played only by those functions whose measure ν\nu given by (2.22) have a support consisting of at most one point.

If ν\nu in (2.21) is a constant function (i.e., ν⁡(ℝ)=0\nu({\mathbb{R}})=0 for the corresponding measure ν\nu) then by (2.22) f≡β+i​π​ν​(−∞)f\equiv\beta+i\pi\nu(-\infty) is a constant function as well, where ν⁡(−∞)∈[0,1]\nu(-\infty)\in[0,1] by (2.23). fθ1,a,θ​(z)=β+i​π​θ1​(1−θ)+θ​log⁡1+a2a−z,f_{{{\mbox{\footnotesize{$\theta_{1},a,\theta$}}}}}(z)=\beta+i\pi\theta_{1}\,(1-\theta)+\theta\,\log\frac{\sqrt{1+a^{2}}}{a-z}\,,

and so we can define an exceptional class of functions in 𝒫∫∩log⁡𝒫{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}\cap\log\mathcal{P} as follows

Δ𝒫∫\displaystyle\Delta_{{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}} ={β+iπθ1(1−θ)+θ⋅log1+a2a−z|θ,θ1∈[0,1],a,β∈ℝ}\displaystyle=\left\{\beta+i\pi\theta_{1}\,(1-\theta)+\theta\cdot\log\frac{\sqrt{1+a^{2}}}{a-z}\ \,\Big|\ \,\theta,\theta_{1}\in[0,1]\,,\ a,\beta\in{\mathbb{R}}\,\right\} (2.28)
={β+iπθ1⋅(1−θ)+θ⋅log1a−z|θ,θ1∈[0,1],a,β∈ℝ}.\displaystyle=\left\{\beta+i\pi\theta_{1}\cdot(1-\theta)+\theta\cdot\log\frac{1}{a-z}\ \,\Big|\ \,\theta,\theta_{1}\in[0,1]\,,\ a,\beta\in{\mathbb{R}}\,\right\}\,.

Our key result is contained in the following theorem.

Theorem 2.4.

Let 𝒫∫∩log⁡𝒫{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}\cap\log\mathcal{P} and Δ𝒫∫\Delta_{{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}} be defined as in (1.16) and (2.28), respectively. In this case Jν​(ℝ)<ν⁡(ℝ)≤1J_{\nu}({\mathbb{R}})<\nu({\mathbb{R}})\leq 1 and for every 0<y1<y2<+∞0<y_{1}<y_{2}<+\infty and 1/ν⁡(ℝ)<p<1/Jν​(ℝ){1}/{\nu({\mathbb{R}})}<p<{1}/{J_{\nu}({\mathbb{R}})}, the following relations hold

2.3. The class 𝒫log\mathcal{P}_{\log}

 

The next characteristic properties of the functions in the class 𝒫log\mathcal{P}_{\log} follow immediately from (1.17) and (2.27).

Theorem 2.5.

A non-constant function φ∈𝒫\varphi\in\mathcal{P} belongs to 𝒫log\mathcal{P}_{\log} iff one of the following conditions holds:

(1)\displaystyle(1) |φ⁡(x+i​y1)|>|φ⁡(x+i​y2)|,x∈ℝ,0<y1<y2<+∞;\displaystyle\qquad\big|\varphi(x+iy_{1})\big|>\big|\varphi(x+iy_{2})\big|\,,\quad x\in{\mathbb{R}}\,,\quad 0<y_{1}<y_{2}<+\infty\,;

(3)\displaystyle(3) |Uφ​(x1,y)Uφ​(x2,y)Vφ​(x1,y)Vφ​(x2,y)|>0,y>0,−∞<x1<x2<+∞;\displaystyle\qquad\begin{vmatrix}U^{\varphi}(x_{1},y)&U^{\varphi}(x_{2},y)\\ V^{\varphi}(x_{1},y)&V^{\varphi}(x_{2},y)\end{vmatrix}>0\,,\quad y>0\,,\quad-\infty<x_{1}<x_{2}<+\infty\,;
(4)\displaystyle(4) Uφ​(x,y)​Uyφ​(x,y)+Vφ​(x,y)​Vyφ​(x,y)<0,x∈ℝ,y>0.\displaystyle\qquad U^{\varphi}(x,y)\,U_{y}^{\varphi}(x,y)+V^{\varphi}(x,y)\,V_{y}^{\varphi}(x,y)<0\,,\quad x\in{\mathbb{R}}\,,\quad y>0\,.

According to the definition (1.17), the corresponding exceptional class of functions in 𝒫log\mathcal{P}_{\log} can be written in the following manner

exp(Δ𝒫∫)={exp⁡(β+i​π​θ1​(1−θ))(a−z)θ|θ,θ1∈[0,1],a,β∈ℝ}.\exp(\Delta_{{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}})=\left\{\frac{\exp\left(\beta+i\pi\theta_{1}\,(1-\theta)\right)}{(a-z)^{\theta}}\ \Big|\ \theta,\theta_{1}\in[0,1]\,,\quad a,\beta\in{\mathbb{R}}\,\right\}\,. (2.32)

In the sequel, for arbitrary function v∈⋃p>1Lp​(ℝ,d​x)v\in\bigcup_{p>1}L_{p}({\mathbb{R}},dx) we use of the notation

where P​∫ℝv⁡(t)t−x​𝑑t\displaystyle P\int_{{\mathbb{R}}}\frac{v(t)}{t-x}\,dt denotes the principal value of the integral, defined as limε↓0∫|t−x|>εv⁡(t)t−x​𝑑t\displaystyle\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow 0}\int_{|t-x|>\varepsilon}\frac{v(t)}{t-x}\,dt\,. Theorem 2.6.

Let 𝒫log\mathcal{P}_{\log}, exp⁡(Δ𝒫∫)\exp(\Delta_{{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}}) and Jν​(ℝ){J}_{\nu}({\mathbb{R}}) be defined as in (1.17), (2.32) and (2.29), respectively. Then:

where the principal branch of the logarithm is taken, β∈ℝ\beta\in{\mathbb{R}} and ν\nu is a non-decreasing function on ℝ{\mathbb{R}} satisfying 0≤ν⁡(x1)≤ν⁡(x2)≤10\leq\nu(x_{1})\leq\nu(x_{2})\leq 1 and −∞<x1<x2<+∞-\infty<x_{1}<x_{2}<+\infty.

For almost all x∈ℝx\in{\mathbb{R}} we have log⁡1+t2|t−x|∈L1​(ℝ,d​ν​(t))\log{{\mbox{\large{$\frac{\sqrt{1+t^{2}}}{\vphantom{A^{A^{a}}}|t-x|}$}}}}\in L_{1}({\mathbb{R}},d\nu(t)) and

2. Let φ∈𝒫log∖exp⁡(Δ𝒫∫)\varphi\in\mathcal{P}_{\log}\setminus\exp(\Delta_{{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}}) and ν\nu be a measure corresponding to φ\varphi in the righthand side of the exponential representation in (2.34). Then Jν​(ℝ)<ν⁡(ℝ)≤1J_{\nu}({\mathbb{R}})<\nu({\mathbb{R}})\leq 1 and for every 1/ν⁡(ℝ)<p<1/Jν​(ℝ){1}/{\nu({\mathbb{R}})}<p<{1}/{J_{\nu}({\mathbb{R}})} and 0<y1<y2<+∞0<y_{1}<y_{2}<+\infty the following inequalities hold

∫−∞+∞|φ⁡(x+i​y2)|p​𝑑x<∫−∞+∞|φ⁡(x+i​y1)|p​𝑑x<∫−∞+∞|φ⁡(x+i​0)|p​𝑑x<+∞\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}|\varphi(x+iy_{2})|^{p}\,dx<\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}|\varphi(x+iy_{1})|^{p}\,dx<\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}|\varphi(x+i0)|^{p}\,dx<+\infty

and

φ⁡(x+i​0)=v~​(x)+i​v​(x)m-a.e. on ℝ,\varphi(x+i0)=\widetilde{v}(x)+iv(x)\quad\text{\rm$m$-a.e. on ${\mathbb{R}}$}\,, (2.36)

where v~​(x),v⁡(x)∈Lp​(ℝ,d​x)\widetilde{v}(x),v(x)\in L_{p}({\mathbb{R}},dx), v​(x):=Vφ​(x)v(x):=V^{\varphi}(x) and v~\widetilde{v} is defined by formula (2.33). In particular,

We observe, that the righthand sides of (2.34) and (2.35) can be written as

The following fact follows easily from Theorem 2.6.

Theorems 2.6 and 2.5 allow to describe the set of functions Im⁡φ\IM\varphi, when φ\varphi runs over the class φ∈𝒫log∖exp⁡(Δ𝒫∫)\varphi\in\mathcal{P}_{\log}\setminus\exp(\Delta_{{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}}).

3. Preliminary Results

3.1. Special properties of Pick functions

 

Taking into account the special importance of the properties (1.8)-(1.10) and (1.19) for the theory of Pick functions, we give here independent simple proofs of these relations.

For this purpose we recall a well-known result in the theory of HpH_{p}-spaces (see [24, p.70], [14, Th.3.1, p.57])

f∈Hp​(𝔻)⇒∃limr↑1f⁡(r​ei​θ)∈Lp​([−π,π],d​θ),0<p<+∞,f\in H_{p}({\mathbb{D}})\quad\Rightarrow\quad\exists\,\lim_{r\uparrow 1}f(re^{i\theta})\in L_{p}([-\pi,\pi],\,d\theta)\,,\quad 0<p<+\infty\,, (3.1)

and observe that each Φ∈𝒫\Phi\in\mathcal{P}, Φ≢a\Phi\not\equiv a, a∈ℝa\in{\mathbb{R}}, is an extension to Hol⁡(ℂ∖ℝ)\hol({\mathbb{C}}\setminus{\mathbb{R}}) of a unique function from the class

𝒫+:={Φ∈Hol⁡(ℍ)∣Φ⁡(ℍ)⊆ℍ},\mathcal{P}_{+}:=\left\{\Phi\in\hol({\mathbb{H}})\mid\Phi({\mathbb{H}})\subseteq{\mathbb{H}}\right\}\,,

by means of the formula Φ⁡(z)=Φ⁡(z¯)¯\Phi(z)=\overline{\Phi(\overline{z})}, z∈−ℍz\in-{\mathbb{H}}.

3.1.1. Proof of (1.8) - (1.10).

Inequalities (1.8) and (1.9) are obviously valid for any constant functions. Thus, it is sufficient to prove them for all functions from 𝒫+\mathcal{P}_{+} and log⁡𝒫+\log\mathcal{P}_{+}, respectively. Two fundamental properties of arbitrary function Φ∈𝒫+\Phi\in\mathcal{P}_{+} are:

f:=log⁡Φ∈𝒫+andIm⁡f=arg⁡Φ∈(0,π).f:=\log\Phi\in\mathcal{P}_{+}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\IM f=\arg\Phi\in(0,\pi)\,.

According to (1.9), exp⁡(|f⁡(x+i​0)|)∈Lδ​([−Λ,Λ],d​x)\exp\big(\,|f(x+i0)|\,\big)\in L_{\delta}\big([-\Lambda,\Lambda],\,dx\big) for arbitrary Λ>0\Lambda>0 and δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1). Obviously,

from which we get the validity of (1.19) by taking the limit as Λ→+∞\Lambda\to+\infty. □\square

3.2. Auxiliary lemma

 

We first prove (1.14). Using (2.7) and the equality μ⁡(1+0)=1\mu(1+0)=1 we get

=∫[0,1]log⁡1−t​z1+t2​d​(1−μ⁡(t))\displaystyle=\int_{[0,1]}\log\frac{1-tz}{\sqrt{1+t^{2}}}\;d(1-\mu(t))
=(1−μ⁡(t))⋅log⁡1−t​z1+t2|0−01+0+∫[0,1](1−μ⁡(t))​d​(12​log⁡(1+t2)−log⁡(1−t​z))\displaystyle=(1-\mu(t))\cdot\left.\log\frac{1-tz}{\sqrt{1+t^{2}}}\right|_{0-0}^{1+0}+\int_{[0,1]}(1-\mu(t))\;d\left({{\mbox{\large{$\frac{1}{\vphantom{A^{A^{a}}}2}$}}}}\log(1+t^{2})-\log(1-tz)\right)

=∫1∞(1−μ⁡(1/t))​(1+z​t)​d​t(t2+1)​(t−z)\displaystyle=\int_{1}^{\infty}(1-\mu(1/t))\,\frac{(1+zt)\;dt}{(t^{2}+1)\,(t-z)}

In order to prove Theorem 2.2 we will need the following assertion.

Lemma 3.1.

Let ν\nu be a non-negative and non-decreasing function on ℝ{\mathbb{R}} satisfying (2.12). Then

  1. (1)

    ∃limt→−∞ν⁡(t)=:ν⁡(−∞)≥0\exists\,\lim_{t\to-\infty}\nu(t)=:\nu(-\infty)\geq 0 ;

  2. (2)

    ∃limt→+∞ν⁡(t)/t=0\exists\,\lim_{t\to+\infty}\nu(t)/t=0 ;

  3. (3)

    (2.15) holds.

Proof.

Statement (1) is trivial. To prove (2) suppose on the contrary that

2​a:=lim¯t→+∞ν​(t)/t>0.2a:=\limsp\limits_{t\to+\infty}\nu(t)/t>0\,.

Then there exists a sequence of monotonically increasing positive numbers

1<t1<t2<⋯<tn<tn+1<…,tn→+∞,n→∞,1<t_{1}<t_{2}<\dots<t_{n}<t_{n+1}<\dots\,,\quad t_{n}\to+\infty\,,\quad n\to\infty\,,

such that

ν⁡(tn)tn≥a,n≥1.\frac{\nu(t_{n})}{t_{n}}\geq a\,,\quad n\geq 1\,.

Since ν\nu is a non-decreasing non-negative function, and in view of the hypothesis (2.12), we have

+∞\displaystyle+\infty >∫1+∞ν⁡(t)​d​tt2≥∫t1+∞ν⁡(t)​d​tt2=∑n=1∞∫tntn+1ν⁡(t)​d​tt2\displaystyle>\int_{1}^{+\infty}\frac{\nu(t)\,dt}{t^{2}}\geq\int_{t_{1}}^{+\infty}\frac{\nu(t)\,dt}{t^{2}}=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n+1}}\frac{\nu(t)\,dt}{t^{2}}
≥∑n=1∞ν⁡(tn)​∫tntn+1d​tt2≥∑n=1∞a⋅tn​(1tn−1tn+1)=a​∑n=1∞(1−tntn+1).\displaystyle\geq\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\nu(t_{n})\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{n+1}}\frac{dt}{t^{2}}\geq\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a\cdot t_{n}\left(\frac{1}{t_{n}}-\frac{1}{t_{n+1}}\right)=a\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(1-\frac{t_{n}}{t_{n+1}}\right)\,.

Whence we have

∑n=1∞θn<+∞,θn:=1−tntn+1∈(0,1),n≥1.\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\theta_{n}<+\infty\,,\quad\theta_{n}:=1-\frac{t_{n}}{t_{n+1}}\in(0,1)\,,\quad n\geq 1\,.

Thus, limn→∞θn=0\lim_{n\to\infty}\theta_{n}=0 and without loss of generality we may assume that θn≤12\theta_{n}\leq\frac{1}{2} for all n≥1n\geq 1. Then, iterating tn+1=tn1−θnt_{n+1}=\frac{t_{n}}{1-\theta_{n}} we get

tn+1=tn1−θn=tn−1(1−θn)​(1−θn−1)=⋯=t1(1−θn)​(1−θn−1)​…​(1−θ1),t_{n+1}=\frac{t_{n}}{1-\theta_{n}}=\frac{t_{n-1}}{(1-\theta_{n})\,(1-\theta_{n-1})}=\dots=\frac{t_{1}}{(1-\theta_{n})\,(1-\theta_{n-1})\dots(1-\theta_{1})}\;,

and

log∏k=1n11−θk=∑k=1nlog(1+θk1−θk)≤∑k=1nθk1−θk≤2∑k=1nθk≤2∑k=1∞θk.\log\prod_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{1-\theta_{k}}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\log\left(1+\frac{\theta_{k}}{1-\theta_{k}}\right)\leq\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{\theta_{k}}{1-\theta_{k}}\leq 2\sum_{k=1}^{n}\theta_{k}\leq 2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\theta_{k}\,.

Therefore

tn+1≤t1⋅e2​∑k=1∞θk,t_{n+1}\leq t_{1}\cdot e^{{{\mbox{\footnotesize{$2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\theta_{k}$}}}}}\,,

in contradiction to the fact that tn→+∞t_{n}\to+\infty as n→∞n\to\infty, and (2) is verified.

In proving (3) it suffices to observe that (2.12) for A>1A>1 implies

+∞\displaystyle+\infty >∫1+∞ν⁡(t)​d​tt2≥∫1Aν⁡(t)​d​tt2=−∫1Aν(t)d1t\displaystyle>\int_{1}^{+\infty}\frac{\nu(t)\,dt}{t^{2}}\geq\int_{1}^{A}\frac{\nu(t)\,dt}{t^{2}}=-\int_{1}^{A}\nu(t)\;d\,\frac{1}{t}
=−ν(t)⋅1t|1A+∫1Ad​ν​(t)t=ν(1)−ν⁡(A)A+∫1Ad​ν​(t)t.\displaystyle=-\left.\nu(t)\cdot\frac{1}{t}\right|_{1}^{A}+\int_{1}^{A}\frac{d\nu(t)}{t}=\nu(1)-\frac{\nu(A)}{A}+\int_{1}^{A}\frac{d\nu(t)}{t}\,.

Using the result of item (2) of this lemma and letting A→+∞A\to+\infty gives

+∞>ν⁡(1)+∫1+∞d​ν​(t)t.+\infty>\nu(1)+\int_{1}^{+\infty}\frac{d\nu(t)}{t}\;.

This completes the proof of Lemma 3.1. ∎

3.3. Particular case of the generalized Hölder inequality

 

In order to prove Theorem 2.4 we need to use a special case of the generalized Hölder inequality established in [26, (11), p.460].

Let ℕ:={1,2,…}{\mathbb{N}}:=\{1,2,\dots\}, ℝ+:=[0,+∞){\mathbb{R}}^{+}:=[0,+\infty), A×B⊂ℝ2A\times B\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{2} the Cartesian product of A,B∈ℬ⁡(ℝ)A,B\in\mathcal{B}({\mathbb{R}}) [32, p.8] and μ1×μ2\mu_{1}\times\mu_{2} the product of μ1,μ2∈ℳ+​(ℝ)\mu_{1},\mu_{2}\in\mathcal{M}^{+}({\mathbb{R}}) [32, p.304].

Lemma 3.2.

Let Ω,Q∈ℬ⁡(ℝ)\Omega,Q\in\mathcal{B}({\mathbb{R}}) be fixed and ρ,ω∈ℳ+​(ℝ)\rho,\omega\in\mathcal{M}^{+}({\mathbb{R}}) such that

0<ρ⁡(Ω)<10<ω⁡(Q)<∞.0<\rho(\Omega)<1\,\quad 0<\omega(Q)<\infty\,. (3.5)

Let furthermore Ψ:Q×Ω→ℝ+∪{+∞}\Psi:Q\times\Omega\to{\mathbb{R}}^{+}\cup\{+\infty\} be a Borel measurable function [34, Def.11.13, p.310] such that Ψ​(x,t)ρ⁡(Ω)∈L1​(Q,d​ω​(x))\Psi(x,t)^{{{\mbox{\footnotesize{$\rho(\Omega)$}}}}}\in L_{1}(Q,d\omega(x)) for all t∈Ωt\in\Omega and

(a)inft∈ΩΨ⁡(x,t)>0,x∈Q;(b)DΨ:=supt∈Ω∫QΨ​(x,t)ρ⁡(Ω)​𝑑ω​(x)<∞.{\rm(a)}\quad\inf_{t\in\Omega}\Psi(x,t)>0\,,\ x\in Q\,;\qquad{\rm(b)}\quad D_{\Psi}:=\sup_{t\in\Omega}\int_{Q}\Psi(x,t)^{{{\mbox{\footnotesize{$\rho(\Omega)$}}}}}\,d\omega(x)<\infty\,. (3.6)

Then log⁡Ψ⁡(x,t)∈L1​(Ω,d​ρ​(t))\log\Psi(x,t)\in L_{1}(\Omega,d\rho(t)) for almost all x∈Qx\in Q with respect to the measure ω\omega and

∫Qexp⁡(∫Ωlog⁡Ψ⁡(x,t)​𝑑ρ​(t))​𝑑ω​(x)≤DΨ.\int_{Q}\exp\left(\int_{\Omega}\log\Psi(x,t)\,d\rho(t)\right)\,d\omega(x)\leq D_{\Psi}\,. (3.7)
Proof.

Let Φ⁡(x,t):=Ψ​(x,t)ρ⁡(Ω)\Phi(x,t):=\Psi(x,t)^{\rho(\Omega)}, γ⁡(x):=min⁡{1,inft∈ΩΦ⁡(x,t)}\gamma(x):=\min\{1,\inf_{t\in\Omega}\Phi(x,t)\} and P⁡(A):=ρ⁡(A)/ρ⁡(Ω)P(A):=\rho(A)/\rho(\Omega), A⊂ΩA\subset\Omega, A∈ℬ⁡(ℝ)A\in\mathcal{B}({\mathbb{R}}). In view of (3.6)(a), γ⁡(x)∈(0,1]\gamma(x)\in(0,1] for all x∈Qx\in Q and therefore we have γ:=∫Qγ⁡(x)​𝑑ω​(x)∈(0,ω⁡(Q)]\gamma:=\int_{Q}\gamma(x)\,d\omega(x)\in(0,\omega(Q)] by (3.5). We introduce the functions

Φn​(x,t):=min⁡{n,Φ⁡(x,t)},φn​(t):=∫QΦn​(u,t)​𝑑ω​(u),x∈Q,t∈Ω,n∈ℕ.\Phi_{n}(x,t):=\min\{n,\Phi(x,t)\}\,,\qquad\varphi_{n}(t):=\int_{Q}\Phi_{n}(u,t)\,d\omega(u)\,,\quad x\in Q\,,\ t\in\Omega\,,\ n\in{\mathbb{N}}\,.

From 0<γ⁡(x)≤Φn​(x,t)≤n0<\gamma(x)\leq\Phi_{n}(x,t)\leq n it follows that for every x∈Qx\in Q and t∈Ωt\in\Omega the following inequalities hold:

−∞<logγ≤logφn(t)≤log(n⋅ω(Q)),−∞<logγ(x)≤logΦn(x,t)≤logn.-\infty<\log\gamma\leq\log\varphi_{n}(t)\leq\log(n\cdot\omega(Q))\,,\qquad-\infty<\log\gamma(x)\leq\log\Phi_{n}(x,t)\leq\log n\,.

Thus, for each n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}} and x∈Qx\in Q, log⁡Φn​(x,t)\log\Phi_{n}(x,t), log⁡φn​(t)∈L1​(Ω,d​P​(t))\log\varphi_{n}(t)\in L_{1}(\Omega,\,dP(t)) and hence it is possible to define the finite-valued functions

hn​(x,t)\displaystyle h_{n}(x,t) :=logΦn(x,t)−log∫QΦn(u,t)dω(u),\displaystyle:=\log\Phi_{n}(x,t)-\log\int_{Q}\Phi_{n}(u,t)\,d\omega(u)\,,
Hn​(x)\displaystyle H_{n}(x) :=∫Ωhn(x,t)dP(t)=∫ΩlogΦn(x,t)dP(t)−∫Ω(log∫QΦn(u,t)dω(u))dP(t),\displaystyle:=\int_{\Omega}h_{n}(x,t)\,dP(t)=\int_{\Omega}\log\Phi_{n}(x,t)\,dP(t)-\int_{\Omega}\left(\log\int_{Q}\Phi_{n}(u,t)\,d\omega(u)\right)\,dP(t)\,,

for all t∈Ωt\in\Omega, x∈Qx\in Q and n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}. Jensen’s inequality [14, Lem.6.1, p.34] applied to the exponential function gives for all x∈Qx\in Q and n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}},

exp⁡(∫Ωhn​(x,t)​𝑑P​(t))\displaystyle\exp\left(\int_{\Omega}h_{n}(x,t)\,dP(t)\right) ≤∫Ωexp⁡(hn​(x,t))​𝑑P​(t)\displaystyle\leq\int_{\Omega}\exp\left(h_{n}(x,t)\right)\,dP(t)
=∫Ωexp(logΦn(x,t)−log∫QΦn(u,t)dω(u))dP(t)\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\exp\left(\log\Phi_{n}(x,t)-\log\int_{Q}\Phi_{n}(u,t)\,d\omega(u)\right)\,dP(t)
=∫Ω[Φn​(x,t)∫QΦn​(u,t)​𝑑ω​(u)]​𝑑P​(t)\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\left[\frac{\Phi_{n}(x,t)}{\int_{Q}\Phi_{n}(u,t)\;d\omega(u)}\right]\,dP(t)
=∫Ω[Φn​(x,t)φn​(t)]​𝑑P​(t),\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\left[\frac{\Phi_{n}(x,t)}{\varphi_{n}(t)}\right]\,dP(t)\,,

i.e.,

eHn​(x)≤∫Ω[Φn​(x,t)∫QΦn​(u,t)​𝑑ω​(u)]​𝑑P​(t)=∫Ω[Φn​(x,t)φn​(t)]​𝑑P​(t),x∈Q,n∈ℕ,e^{H_{n}(x)}\leq\int_{\Omega}\left[\frac{\Phi_{n}(x,t)}{\int_{Q}\Phi_{n}(u,t)\,d\omega(u)}\right]\,dP(t)=\int_{\Omega}\left[\frac{\Phi_{n}(x,t)}{\varphi_{n}(t)}\right]\,dP(t)\,,\quad x\in Q\,,\ n\in{\mathbb{N}}\,, (3.8)

where the function Φn​(x,t)/φn​(t)\Phi_{n}(x,t)/\varphi_{n}(t), being positive and bounded above by n/γn/\gamma on Q×ΩQ\times\Omega, belongs to L1​(Q×Ω,d⁡(ω×P)​(x,t))L_{1}(Q\times\Omega,d(\omega\times P)(x,t)). Integrating (3.8) over x∈Qx\in Q with respect to the measure ω\omega we obtain by Fubini’s theorem [32, p.307]

∫QeHn​(x)​𝑑ω​(x)≤∫Q∫ΩΦn​(x,t)∫QΦn​(u,t)​𝑑ω​(u)​𝑑P​(t)​𝑑ω​(x)=∫Ω∫QΦn​(x,t)​𝑑ω​(x)∫QΦn​(u,t)​𝑑ω​(u)​𝑑P​(t)=1,\int_{Q}e^{H_{n}(x)}\,d\omega(x)\leq\int_{Q}\int_{\Omega}\frac{\Phi_{n}(x,t)}{\int_{Q}\Phi_{n}(u,t)\,d\omega(u)}\;dP(t)\,d\omega(x)=\int_{\Omega}\dfrac{\int_{Q}\Phi_{n}(x,t)\,d\omega(x)}{\int_{Q}\Phi_{n}(u,t)\,d\omega(u)}\;dP(t)=1\,,

from which it follows that

∫Qexp{∫ΩlogΦn(x,t)dP(t)−∫Ω(log∫QΦn(u,t)dω(u))dP(t)}dω(x)≤1,\int_{Q}\exp\left\{\int_{\Omega}\log\Phi_{n}(x,t)\,dP(t)-\int_{\Omega}\left(\log\int_{Q}\Phi_{n}(u,t)\,d\omega(u)\right)\,dP(t)\right\}\,d\omega(x)\leq 1\,,

i.e.,

∫Qexp{∫ΩlogΦn(x,t)dP(t)}dω(x)≤exp{∫Ω(log∫QΦn(u,t)dω(u))dP(t)}.\int_{Q}\exp\left\{\int_{\Omega}\log\Phi_{n}(x,t)\,dP(t)\right\}\;d\omega(x)\leq\exp\left\{\int_{\Omega}\left(\log\int_{Q}\Phi_{n}(u,t)\;d\omega(u)\right)\,dP(t)\right\}\,.

Applying Jensen’s inequality to the right-hand side of the last inequality we obtain

∫Qexp\displaystyle\int_{Q}\exp {∫ΩlogΦn(x,t)dP(t)}dω(x)≤∫Ωexp(log∫QΦn(u,t)dω(u))dP(t)\displaystyle\left\{\int_{\Omega}\log\Phi_{n}(x,t)\,dP(t)\right\}\,d\omega(x)\leq\int_{\Omega}\exp\left(\log\int_{Q}\Phi_{n}(u,t)\,d\omega(u)\right)dP(t)
=∫Ω(∫QΦn​(u,t)​𝑑ω​(u))​𝑑P​(t)≤∫Ω(∫QΦ⁡(u,t)​𝑑ω​(u))​𝑑P​(t)\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\left(\int_{Q}\Phi_{n}(u,t)\,d\omega(u)\right)\,dP(t)\leq\int_{\Omega}\left(\int_{Q}\Phi(u,t)\,d\omega(u)\right)\,dP(t)
=∫Ω(∫QΨ​(u,t)ρ⁡(Ω)​𝑑ω​(u))​𝑑P​(t)≤∫ΩDΨ​𝑑P​(t)=DΨ.\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\left(\int_{Q}\Psi(u,t)^{\rho(\Omega)}\,d\omega(u)\right)\,dP(t)\leq\int_{\Omega}D_{\Psi}\,dP(t)=D_{\Psi}\,.

Summarizing, we have obtained the upper bound

∫Ωexp⁡(∫Ωlog⁡Φn​(x,t)​𝑑P​(t))​𝑑ω​(x)≤DΨ,n∈ℕ.\int_{\Omega}\exp\left(\int_{\Omega}\log\Phi_{n}(x,t)\;dP(t)\right)\,d\omega(x)\leq D_{\Psi}\,,\quad n\in{\mathbb{N}}\,. (3.9)

Inequalities 0<γ⁡(x)≤Φn​(x,t)≤Φm​(x,t)≤m0<\gamma(x)\leq\Phi_{n}(x,t)\leq\Phi_{m}(x,t)\leq m, which are valid for all (x,t)∈Q×Ω(x,t)\in Q\times\Omega and m≥n≥1m\geq n\geq 1, yield that Φn​(x,t)\Phi_{n}(x,t), log⁡Φn​(x,t)\log\Phi_{n}(x,t) and exp⁡(∫Ωlog⁡Φn​(x,t)​𝑑P​(t))\exp\big(\int_{\Omega}\log\Phi_{n}(x,t)\,dP(t)\big), n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}, are pointwise monotone non-decreasing sequences of finite-valued measurable functions. Hence, their limits as n→∞n\to\infty exist, regardless of whether they are finite or equal to +∞+\infty. Furthermore, the first two of these limits equal to Φ⁡(x,t)\Phi(x,t) and log⁡Φ⁡(x,t)\log\Phi(x,t), respectively. Now let us define:

ψ⁡(x):=limn→∞∫Ωlog⁡Φn​(x,t)​𝑑P​(t),x∈Q.\psi(x):=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{\Omega}\log\Phi_{n}(x,t)\,dP(t)\,,\quad x\in Q\,.

It is clear that for each x∈Qx\in Q

−∞<log⁡γ⁡(x)=∫Ωlog⁡γ⁡(x)​𝑑P​(t)≤∫Ωlog⁡Φn​(x,t)​𝑑P​(t)≤limn→∞∫Ωlog⁡Φn​(x,t)​𝑑P​(t)=ψ⁡(x).-\infty<\log\gamma(x)=\int_{\Omega}\log\gamma(x)\,dP(t)\leq\int_{\Omega}\log\Phi_{n}(x,t)\;dP(t)\leq\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{\Omega}\log\Phi_{n}(x,t)\;dP(t)=\psi(x)\,.

Beppo Levi’s theorem [23, p.305] applied to the inequalities (3.9) gives

∫Qexp⁡(ψ⁡(x))​𝑑ω​(x)\displaystyle\int_{Q}\exp\left(\psi(x)\right)\;d\omega(x) =∫Qexp⁡(limn→∞∫Ωlog⁡Φn​(x,t)​𝑑P​(t))​𝑑ω​(x)\displaystyle=\int_{Q}\exp\left(\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{\Omega}\log\Phi_{n}(x,t)\,dP(t)\right)\,d\omega(x)
=∫Qlimn→∞exp⁡(∫Ωlog⁡Φn​(x,t)​𝑑P​(t))​𝑑ω​(x)\displaystyle=\int_{Q}\lim_{n\to\infty}\exp\left(\int_{\Omega}\log\Phi_{n}(x,t)\,dP(t)\right)\,d\omega(x)
=limn→∞∫Qexp⁡(∫Ωlog⁡Φn​(x,t)​𝑑P​(t))​𝑑ω​(x)≤DΨ,\displaystyle=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{Q}\exp\left(\int_{\Omega}\log\Phi_{n}(x,t)\,dP(t)\right)\,d\omega(x)\leq D_{\Psi}\ ,

i.e., summarizing,

∫Ωexp⁡(ψ⁡(x))​𝑑ω​(x)≤DΨ,x∈Q.\int_{\Omega}\exp\big(\psi(x)\big)\;d\omega(x)\leq D_{\Psi}\,,\quad x\in Q\,. (3.10)

Let Qψ∞:={x∈Q∣ψ⁡(x)=+∞}Q_{\psi}^{\infty}:=\big\{x\in Q\mid\psi(x)=+\infty\big\} and Q^:=Q∖Qψ∞\widehat{Q}:=Q\setminus Q_{\psi}^{\infty}. Then (3.10) implies that ω⁡(Qψ∞)=0\omega\left(Q_{\psi}^{\infty}\right)=0.

Now, for each fixed x∈Q^x\in\widehat{Q} one can again apply Beppo Levi’s theorem [23, p.305] to the non-decreasing sequence of integrable functions n≥log⁡Φn​(x,⋅)>log⁡γ⁡(x)>−∞n\geq\log\Phi_{n}(x,\cdot)>\log\gamma(x)>-\infty, n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}, satisfying

−∞<log⁡γ⁡(x)≤∫Ωlog⁡Φn​(x,t)​𝑑P​(t)≤ψ⁡(x)<+∞,-\infty<\log\gamma(x)\leq\int_{\Omega}\log\Phi_{n}(x,t)\;dP(t)\leq\psi(x)<+\infty\,,

to get log⁡Φ⁡(x,t)∈L1​(Ω,d​P​(t))\log\Phi(x,t)\in L_{1}(\Omega,dP(t)),

∫Ωlog⁡Φ⁡(x,t)​𝑑P​(t)=∫Ωlimn→∞log⁡Φn​(x,t)​𝑑P​(t)=limn→∞∫Ωlog⁡Φn​(x,t)​𝑑P​(t)=ψ⁡(x)<+∞,\int_{\Omega}\log\Phi(x,t)\,dP(t)=\int_{\Omega}\lim_{n\to\infty}\log\Phi_{n}(x,t)\,dP(t)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{\Omega}\log\Phi_{n}(x,t)\,dP(t)=\psi(x)<+\infty\;,

and hence, log⁡Ψ⁡(x,t)∈L1​(Ω,d​ρ​(t))\log\Psi(x,t)\in L_{1}(\Omega,d\rho(t)). Thus,

ψ⁡(x)=∫Ωlog⁡Φ⁡(x,t)​𝑑P​(t)=∫Ωlog⁡Ψ⁡(x,t)​𝑑ρ​(t).\psi(x)=\int_{\Omega}\log\Phi(x,t)\,dP(t)=\int_{\Omega}\log\Psi(x,t)\,d\rho(t)\,.

Substitution of the last expression for ψ\psi in (3.10) proves (3.7) and completes the proof of Lemma 3.2. ∎

4. Proofs of the main assertions

4.1. Proof of Theorem 2.1

4.1.1. Proof of item 1.

For a non-negative function VV, which is harmonic in the upper half plane ℍ{\mathbb{H}}, the following well known representation holds (see [24, p.107], [10, Th.II, p.20]): there exists a measure σ∈ℳ+​(ℝ)\sigma\in\mathcal{M}^{+}({\mathbb{R}}) with

∫−∞+∞d​σ​(t)1+t2<+∞,\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\frac{d\sigma(t)}{1+t^{2}}<+\infty\,, (4.1)

and a constant α≥0\alpha\geq 0 such that

4.1.2. Proof of item 2.

Since Vx​(x,y)V_{x}(x,y) is a non-negative function harmonic in ℍ{\mathbb{H}} it follows from the mean value property of harmonic functions [18, (1.5.4), p.34] that either Vx​(x,y)>0V_{x}(x,y)>0 or Vx​(x,y)=0V_{x}(x,y)=0 everywhere in ℍ{\mathbb{H}}.

Assume that Vx​(x,y)≡0V_{x}(x,y)\equiv 0 in ℍ{\mathbb{H}}. Then, the leftmost integral in (4.7) would be zero and hence equality would be attained in (4.8) for all −∞<x1<x2<+∞-\infty<x_{1}<x_{2}<+\infty. As σ⁡(x)\sigma(x) is nondecreasing and finite on ℝ{\mathbb{R}}, this means by [17, 111, p.91] that σ⁡(t)=a​t+b\sigma(t)=at+b for some a≥0a\geq 0 and b∈ℝb\in{\mathbb{R}}. Using (4.2) and (4.9) we get V⁡(x,y)=α​y+a⋅πV(x,y)=\alpha y+a\cdot\pi and ν⁡(x)≡a\nu(x)\equiv a for all y>0y>0 and x∈ℝx\in{\mathbb{R}}, as stated in Theorem 2.1. Conversely, if ν≡a≥0\nu\equiv a\geq 0 then we get from (2.10) that V⁡(x,y)=α​y+a⋅πV(x,y)=\alpha y+a\cdot\pi and so Vx​(x,y)≡0V_{x}(x,y)\equiv 0. Finally, if for some α,a≥0\alpha,a\geq 0 we have V⁡(x,y)=α​y+a⋅πV(x,y)=\alpha y+a\cdot\pi for all y>0y>0 and x∈ℝx\in{\mathbb{R}}, then the uniqueness of the representation (2.10) proved above gives ν≡a\nu\equiv a. The proof is complete. □\Box

4.2. Proof of Theorem 2.2

4.2.1. Proof of item 1.

If Φ∈𝒫∫∩𝒫⊂𝒫\Phi\in\mathcal{P}_{\int}\cap\mathcal{P}\subset\mathcal{P}, then according to [10, Th.II, p.20] it has a unique canonical representation of the form (1.3) and V=VΦV=V^{\Phi} satisfies the conditions of Theorem 2.1. Since the measure σ\sigma is completely determined by the function VΦV^{\Phi} [10, Th.II, p.21], applying Theorem 2.1 we get the representation (2.13) for Φ\Phi. Conversely, a function Φ\Phi with the integral representation (2.13) has an imaginary part VV with the representation (2.10) and therefore Φ∈𝒫∫∩𝒫\Phi\in\mathcal{P}_{\int}\cap\mathcal{P}, due to the results of Theorem 2.1.

In view of (2.4) and (2.5) it is possible to replace ν\nu in (2.13) and (2.14) by an arbitrary function from the class ℵν\aleph_{\,\nu} defined in (2.4). Since (2.13) is a particular case of the unique representation (1.3) and (2.14) is equivalent to (2.13) we get the uniqueness of (2.13) and (2.14) provided that all functions in ℵν\aleph_{\,\nu} are identified.

4.4. Proofs of Theorem 2.3 and Corollary 2.2

4.4.1. Proof of Theorem 2.3.

Note first that any function f∈𝒫∫∩log⁡𝒫f\in{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}\cap\log\mathcal{P} belongs to the intersectio of the classes 𝒫∫∩𝒫{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}\cap\mathcal{P} and log⁡𝒫\log\mathcal{P}. Therefore the results of Theorem 2.2 and the representations (1.3) and (1.5) are valid for ff. Uniqueness of the representation (1.3) for ff together with the possibility of writing it in both forms (2.13) and (1.5) implies immediately the representation (2.21) with ν\nu satisfying (2.23). All other statements of Theorem 2.3 except the last three ones are direct consequences of the corresponding statements of Theorem 2.2. The last three statements of Theorem 2.3 follow from (2.23), Theorem 2.2, 4) and the additional remark that a linear function belongs to log⁡𝒫\log\mathcal{P} if and only if it is the constant one, as it follows from the inequalities 0≤Im⁡φ⁡(z)≤π0\leq\IM\varphi(z)\leq\pi, z∈ℍz\in{\mathbb{H}}, for arbitrary φ∈log⁡𝒫\varphi\in\log\mathcal{P}.

Using Theorem 2.3 for f:=log⁡φf:=\log\varphi we get (see [10, p.27]) that ff is a non-constant function in the class log⁡𝒫\log\mathcal{P}, φ=ef\varphi=e^{f} and

4.7. Proofs of Theorem 2.6 and Corollary 2.3

4.7.1. Proof of Theorem 2.6.

Observe that the first item of Theorem 2.6 follows directly from Theorem 2.3 and (1.17). If φ∈𝒫log∖exp⁡Δ𝒫∫\varphi\in\mathcal{P}_{\log}\setminus\exp{\Delta_{{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}}} then φ=ef\varphi=e^{f}, where f∈(𝒫∫∩log⁡𝒫)∖Δ𝒫∫f\in\left({\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}\cap\log\mathcal{P}\right)\setminus\Delta_{{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}}. Using the notation of Theorems 2.3 and 2.5 we can apply the results of Theorem 2.4 to the function ff in order to get with the help of the relations (4.30) and (4.31) the validity of all statements of Theorem 2.6 except (2.36). Equality (2.36) holds true due to the well-known consequence of M.Riesz’s theorem [24, p.128].

4.7.2. Proof of Corollary 2.3.

If φ⁡(z)=ef\varphi(z)=e^{f}, where f=∫01log⁡11−t​z​𝑑μ​(t)f=\int_{0}^{1}\log\frac{1}{1-tz}\,d\mu(t), then by Corollary 2.2 f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0, f∈Hol⁡((,,,))f\in\hol((-\infty,1)) and f∈𝒫∫∩log⁡𝒫f\in{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}\cap\log\mathcal{P}, which imply the validity of all statements of Corollary 2.3.

Conversely, assume that φ⁡(0)=1\varphi(0)=1, φ∈Hol⁡((,,,))\varphi\in\hol((-\infty,1)) and φ∈𝒫log\varphi\in\mathcal{P}_{\log}. Then there exists f∈𝒫∫∩log⁡𝒫f\in{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}\cap\log\mathcal{P} such that φ⁡(z)=ef\varphi(z)=e^{f} and f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0. Since φ∈𝒫\varphi\in\mathcal{P} and φ∈Hol⁡((,,,))\varphi\in\hol((-\infty,1)) the property (1.4) and representation (1.3) imply that Im⁡φ⁡(x+i0)=0\IM\varphi(x+i0)=0 for any x<1x<1. Then it follows from (2.3) that the function ν\nu corresponding to φ\varphi by the exponential representation (2.34) satisfies sin⁡π​ν​(x)=0\sin\pi\nu(x)=0 for almost all x<1x<1. Since by Theorem 2.6 ν\nu is a nondecreasing function on ℝ{\mathbb{R}} with values in [0,1][0,1] then for almost all x<1x<1 either ν⁡(x)=0\nu(x)=0 or ν⁡(x)=1\nu(x)=1 or ν(x)=χ[a,+∞)(x)\nu(x)=\chi_{[a,+\infty)}(x) for some a<1a<1.

Assume that ν⁡(x)=1\nu(x)=1 for almost all x<1x<1. Then ν⁡(x)≡1\nu(x)\equiv 1 on ℝ{\mathbb{R}} and in view of (2.34), φ⁡(z)\varphi(z) is a constant function and so ff is constant as well. By Corollary 2.2 f≡0f\equiv 0 and ff can be represented in the form (2.26), from which (2.39) follows.

4.8. Proof of Theorem 2.7

4.8.1. Necessity.

Applying the results of Theorem 2.6, 2) to φ∈𝒫log∖exp⁡Δ𝒫∫\varphi\in\mathcal{P}_{\log}\setminus\exp{\Delta_{{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}}} we get the existence of 1<p<+∞1<p<+\infty such that φ∈ℋp​(ℍ)\varphi\in\mathcal{H}_{p}\,({\mathbb{H}}), φ⁡(x+i​0)=v~​(x)+i​v​(x)\varphi(x+i0)=\widetilde{v}(x)+iv(x) for almost all x∈ℝx\in{\mathbb{R}} and v,v~∈Lp​(ℝ,d​x)v,\widetilde{v}\in L_{p}({\mathbb{R}},dx). 4.9. Proof of Theorem 2.8

 

Observe first that if vv satisfies (2.46a) inequality (2.46c) holds for arbitrary −∞<x1<x2<1-\infty<x_{1}<x_{2}<1 and −∞<x1<1<x2<+∞-\infty<x_{1}<1<x_{2}<+\infty. Therefore to check the validity of (2.40) for vv satisfying (2.46a), it suffices to prove it only for all 1<x1<x2<+∞1<x_{1}<x_{2}<+\infty.

4.9.1. Necessity.

Let Ψ\Psi be universally starlike and φ⁡(z):=Ψ⁡(z)/z\varphi(z):=\Psi(z)/z. Then by (1.1) φ⁡(z)\varphi(z) can be represented in the form (2.39) where the measure μ\mu corresponds to φ\varphi. According to Corollary 2.3, φ∈𝒫log\varphi\in\mathcal{P}_{\log}. If φ∈exp⁡Δ𝒫∫\varphi\in\exp{\Delta_{{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}}}, then by virtue of (2.44) φ\varphi belongs to the set in (2.45). Otherwise, φ∈𝒫log∖exp⁡Δ𝒫∫\varphi\in\mathcal{P}_{\log}\setminus\exp{\Delta_{{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}}}. In this case, due to Theorem 2.7, we can find p>1p>1 and v∈Lp​(ℝ,d​x)v\in L_{p}({\mathbb{R}},dx) such that the representation (2.47) holds, v⁡(x)≥0v(x)\geq 0 for all x∈ℝx\in{\mathbb{R}}, vv satisfies (2.46c) and in view of (2.42), φ⁡(x+i​0)=v~​(x)+i​v​(x)\varphi(x+i0)=\widetilde{v}(x)+iv(x) mm-a.e. on ℝ{\mathbb{R}}. Corollary 2.3 states also that φ∈Hol⁡((,,,))\varphi\in\hol((-\infty,1)) and φ⁡(0)=1\varphi(0)=1. Since φ∈𝒫\varphi\in\mathcal{P} we can apply (1.4) and (1.3) to φ∈Hol⁡((,,,))\varphi\in\hol((-\infty,1)) and get v⁡(x)=Im⁡φ⁡(x+i0)=0v(x)=\IM\varphi(x+i0)=0 for any x<1x<1. This finishes the proof of (2.46a). Finally, (2.46b) follows from (2.47) and φ⁡(0)=1\varphi(0)=1.

4.9.2. Sufficiency.

Let Ψ\Psi belong to the set (2.48). Then it follows from (2.44) that Ψ⁡(z)/z\Psi(z)/z can be represented in the form of (2.39) and therefore by (1.1) Ψ\Psi is universally starlike.

Assume now that Ψ\Psi is represented in the form (2.49). Then by Theorem 2.7 Ψ⁡(z)/z∈𝒫log∖exp⁡Δ𝒫∫\Psi(z)/z\in\mathcal{P}_{\log}\setminus\exp{\Delta_{{\mathcal{P}}_{\!\scriptscriptstyle\int}}} and it follows directly from (2.49) and (2.46b) that Ψ⁡(z)/z∈Hol⁡((−∞,1))\Psi(z)/z\in\hol((-\infty,1)) and Ψ′​(0)=1\Psi^{\,\prime}(0)=1, respectively. By Corollary 2.3 this means that Ψ⁡(z)/z\Psi(z)/z can be represented in the form of (2.39) and therefore by (1.1) Ψ\Psi is universally starlike. The proof of Theorem 2.8 is complete.
